title: Phone operating: SSB and sidebands
blurb: Explain why SSB is the HF voice mode, pick LSB or USB by band, break into contacts, and set mic gain.

G2A01.why: At **14 MHz and up** the habit is **upper sideband**.
G2A01.trap: Lower sideband is the habit on the low bands.

G2A02.why: On **160, 75 and 40 m** the habit is **lower sideband**.
G2A02.trap: Upper sideband is the habit from 14 MHz up.

G2A03.why: VHF and UHF SSB follows the high-band habit: **upper sideband**.

G2A04.why: 17 m and 12 m are above 14 MHz, so they use the **upper sideband**.

G2A05.why: **Single sideband** is the most common HF voice mode: narrow and power-efficient.
G2A05.trap: FM is mainly a VHF/UHF mode, and DSB is wider.

G2A06.why: Dropping the carrier and one sideband gives **less bandwidth** and **greater power efficiency**.

G2A07.why: SSB transmits **one sideband**. The **other sideband and the carrier are suppressed**.
G2A07.trap: Keeping the carrier describes a different mode.

G2A08.why: Say your **call sign once**. Long calls and slang just add to the noise.
G2A08.trap: "QRZ" asks who is calling. "CQ" starts a new call.

G2A09.why: No rule or efficiency difference decides it. LSB on these bands is **commonly accepted amateur practice**.
G2A09.trap: Both sidebands are legal on these bands.

G2A10.why: **VOX** keys the transmitter from your voice, so it allows **hands-free** operation.
G2A10.trap: VOX changes neither audio quality, bandwidth nor power.

G2A11.why: **CQ DX** asks for **distant** stations: for a lower-48 caller, any station **outside the lower 48**.

G2A12.why: ALC reads your drive level, set with **transmit audio (mic) gain**.
G2A12.trap: Antenna tuning and attenuators don't set drive level.
